Subject: Initial ask: egress mapping + firewall proof for private endpoints

Hi Connor / team,

Thanks again for the walkthrough this morning. As part of our security review (SOC 2 in Q4) we need a detailed mapping of the egress surface for Redwood's private endpoint offering when deployed into an on-prem environment. Specifically we need: 

- A compact allowlist of destination IPs/CIDRs and hostnames the private endpoint(s) will contact (control plane, telemetry, update checks).
- Expected ports and protocols (e.g., 443/TCP, 53/UDP for DNS, any outbound health check ports).
- Clarification on whether TLS SNI or plaintext Host headers can leak internal service names and how you mitigate this.
- Guidance for customers using egress-proxy (forward proxy) vs egress via an egress-only NAT gateway. Any preferred config examples.
- Required NAT/static IP ranges (we need to add these to our perimeter firewall allowlist) and fallback behaviors if those IPs are unreachable.

Can you attach a short matrix and a sample minimal firewall rule-set we can give our network ops team? Preferably a one-page PDF + spreadsheet matrix.

Attachments: redwood-egress-matrix.xlsx, network-diagram-v2.pdf (we uploaded these to the ticket but would appreciate a formal sign-off doc).

Timeline: we'd like this in hand by EOD Monday (2026-08-24) to stay on schedule for the audit prep.

Thanks,
Priya Rao
Security Program Manager
Acme Corp

Subject: Re: Initial ask: egress mapping + firewall proof for private endpoints

Hi Priya — thanks for the clear checklist. Attaching a concise proposal that covers the minimal allowlist and two deployment patterns (proxy-forwarded egress vs egress-only NAT). See attachment: 20260820-connor-egress-proposal.txt.

High-level summary (so your ops team can skim):
- Control plane (required): outbound TLS (443) to: 34.198.12.0/24, 52.14.33.128/26 and hostnames control.redwood.ai, telemetry.redwood.ai; mTLS optional but strongly recommended for customers that require identity-bound control plane connections.
- Telemetry & metrics: TCP 443 to telemetry.redwood.ai (same IPs above) or routed via customer forward proxy (see proxy rules below).
- DNS: customers MUST allow outbound DNS to their internal recursive resolvers; if you have DNS egress filtering, allow queries to 8.8.8.8/1? Not required — we recommend forwarding to internal resolvers to preserve split-horizon.
- Health checks & updates: outbound HTTPS to update.redwood.ai on 443; we do not use port 80 for any control traffic.
- SNI leakage: if the customer terminates TLS at a forward proxy (TLS interception), SNI may be visible to the proxy. If you need to prevent SNI exposure, configure a TLS tunnel (TCP port 443) to an egress NAT plus IP allowlist and use mTLS to the control plane.

Sample minimal firewall rules (ordered):
1) Allow outbound TCP/443 -> 34.198.12.0/24 (control plane)
2) Allow outbound TCP/443 -> 52.14.33.128/26 (telemetry)
3) Allow outbound TCP/443 -> update.redwood.ai (CNAME to above ranges)
4) Allow DNS -> internal_resolver_ip (UDP/53) only; do not permit arbitrary outbound DNS to internet unless required
5) Deny outbound HTTP (80) to control.redwood.ai and update.redwood.ai

Notes: we provide an optional static egress IP pool you can NAT to if you need fixed source IPs for your perimeter rules. That pool can be provisioned per-customer for Dedicated/Private.

Can Sergio and Marissa weigh in on hairpin/NAT behavior for on-prem installs and whether we should advertise an additional port 8443 for internal health-checks? I'll follow up with a cleaned PDF for your ticket by tomorrow.

—Connor
Connor O'Brien
Technical Account Lead, Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Initial ask: egress mapping + firewall proof for private endpoints

Priya / team — quick technical clarifications to add to Connor's note: 

1) NAT & hairpinning: For on-prem deployments where the private endpoint is inside the same network as services referencing it, customers should avoid hairpin NAT for control plane egress. Preferred pattern is to route egress to an egress-only NAT gateway (one-directional) that has static source IP(s). That prevents asymmetric return-paths and simplifies firewall state.

2) DNS considerations: If your network enforces DNS egress filtering and you use DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) proxies, ensure the forward proxy preserves EDNS and split-horizon answers. If you cannot guarantee that, we recommend configuring the private endpoint to use customer-recursive resolvers only (UDP/53) and whitelist those resolver IPs.

3) Ports: We use TCP/443 for all control/telemetry/update traffic. We do not require inbound ports on customer firewalls. Port 53 (UDP) for DNS only. Internal health-checks can be on 8443 but only when you run the optional agent (agent is not required for control plane).

4) SNI & TLS intercept: If your proxy does TLS terminate+re-encrypt, SNI will be visible to the proxy. mTLS between the private endpoint and control.redwood.ai removes that risk (client cert presented at TLS handshake). If your compliance team prohibits any SNI exposure, we will require an mTLS setup; we can provide cert provisioning guidance.

5) Static egress IPs: we can lease a /29 for your environment for Dedicated/private (per customer). If you need more, we can escalate to Procurement. Static IPs are the easiest way for you to configure perimeter allowlists.

I'll add a short appendix paragraph about EDNS/DoH and proxy behavior to the PDF Connor is preparing. Also linking our internal appendix for your team: https://redwood-internal/docs/vpc-egress-profiles#appendix

Sergio
Senior Infrastructure Engineer | Redwood Inference
